text:
jordan lee: Hi folks, newbie question — my service can't connect to Redis when I run `docker compose up`. The app logs show `ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:6379`. I expected `redis:6379` to be reachable. I'm on mac (Monterey) and didn't change the repo compose file. Any quick debugging tips?

jordan lee: compose.yml (trimmed):
```yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    environment:
      - REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379/0
  redis:
    image: redis:6.2
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
```

jordan lee: I did `docker compose up --build` and it shows redis starting, but the app still hits 127.0.0.1 not `redis` for some reason. :thinking_face:

maya singh: welcome jordan! quick question: are you running the app from your host or inside the container? If you run the app locally (outside compose) and the env var is missing, it might default to localhost. Can you `docker compose exec api env | grep REDIS` to confirm the container has the right var?

jordan lee: good call — I was actually running `cargo run` from my host while compose was up. the env var was set in compose but not in my host shell. I exported REDIS_URL locally to point at 127.0.0.1 and then started the app, but still got connection refused.

chris fong: if you run the app on host and want to talk to the containerized redis via localhost, mapping `6379:6379` should work unless another redis is already listening on the host. Run `lsof -iTCP:6379 -sTCP:LISTEN` to see if something else owns the port (Homebrew Redis, macOS service, etc.). Also check `docker compose ps` to ensure redis is actually bound.

jordan lee: ran `lsof` and it shows `/usr/local/bin/redis-server` bound to TCP *:6379. I had previously installed redis with brew and forgot. So my app was connecting to the host Redis, not the container.

maya singh: yep that explains it — port mapping makes container redis available on the host port 6379, but if host has a process already, docker can't bind and will either fail the mapping or pick a different behavior depending on compose. Usually compose will fail to start the container or the container starts but mapping isn't applied. Check `docker compose logs redis` for bind errors.

jordan lee: `docker compose logs redis` had a bind error earlier but I missed it. Good catch. What's the usual workflow? Should I stop brew redis or change compose ports?

chris fong: for local dev we prefer not to rely on host ports. Two options: 1) stop the host redis (`brew services stop redis`) and keep `ports: - "6379:6379"`, 2) remove the ports mapping and let the api container talk to redis over the internal compose network (recommended). If you remove the `ports` stanza, the redis container is still reachable by service name (`redis:6379`) from other containers but not from your host. Since you're running the app on the host, either export REDIS_URL to point at the docker host IP (localhost) after ensuring docker's redis is bound, or run the app inside the `api` container for parity.

jordan lee: ah. I didn't realize services talk by name without ports exposed. I removed the `ports` line and changed my workflow to run the app in the container: `docker compose run --service-ports api sh -c "cargo run"`. That worked and `redis:6379` was reachable.

maya singh: nice! another developer-friendly trick: add a `compose.override.yml` for local-only mappings and document the `brew services stop redis` in the README so new hires don't hit that. We also sometimes set `container_name` or network aliases for clarity, though not necessary.

compose-bot: Heads-up: new-hires checklist — dev environment tips and `compose.override.yml` example are at https://redwood.internal/devenv/compose. If you need the example snippet ping #devex.

jordan lee: Thanks everyone — saved me a headache. I'll update the onboarding doc with the brew stop note. :pray:
